name: The Burnside Sycamore

location.address: Southwest of Burnside Bridge, Historic Burnside Bridge Road, Sharpsburg, Washington County, Maryland
location.neighbourhood: Beside Burnside Bridge (Antietam National Battlefield), a short walk from the Burnside Bridge parking area

access: Free, within Antietam National Battlefield; grows right beside the Burnside Bridge parking area and the bridge itself, on a flat, short, public path.
transport: No public transit; short drive from Sharpsburg, MD. Parking at the Burnside Bridge lot.
verify_notes: The single most identifiable witness tree at Antietam. Civil War photographer Alexander Gardner photographed it as a young sapling beside the bridge in the days immediately after the Battle of Antietam, 17 September 1862 (the single bloodiest day in American history), and that dated photograph is the documentary basis for its identity: this is a Library of Congress HALS (Historic American Landscapes Survey, a federal record) entry, MD-1748, confirming the tree's identity and location by name (Burnside Bridge Sycamore). It is part of the NPS's own Witness Tree Protection Program. Two further independent sources (American Forest Foundation, American Battlefield Trust) both describe it as alive and thriving today despite creek flooding and a root system constrained by the bridge. No published girth or precise age figure found this pass (age given here is simply years since 1862, since it was already a sapling then, i.e. a minimum bound, not a derived dendrological estimate); flag for a future pass to get a measured circumference if one has been published. Alive: multiple sources, most recent ones (Forest Foundation blog, Tree Care Industry trade piece) describe current condition as healthy and growing.

name: The West Woods Witness Oaks

location.address: The West Woods, Antietam National Battlefield, Sharpsburg, Maryland
location.neighbourhood: West Woods, on a stretch of the battlefield acquired by the park more recently than the surrounding land, near where the 59th New York Infantry stood during Sedgwick's attack on 17 September 1862

access: Free, within Antietam National Battlefield; reachable via the West Woods Trail, a public walking trail with numbered interpretive stops.
transport: No public transit; short drive from Sharpsburg, MD. Parking at the battlefield visitor center or trailhead pull-offs.
verify_notes: Two white oaks standing together (a third, nearby witness tree of unspecified species at the same spot has already died and remains standing, per both sources; not delivered as its own entry since it is dead). HistoryNet's Trees: Silent Survivors piece, which reads as a professional Civil War history publication quoting a park source (a Calzarette, likely NPS staff) on tree condition and a life-expectancy estimate, independently corroborates a personal battlefield-walking blog's account from 2009 of the same three-tree group: two healthy white oaks and one dead standing tree, on land the park acquired relatively recently, positioned near where the 59th New York Infantry stood as Jubal Early's Confederate brigade rushed past during Sedgwick's attack in the West Woods. Both oaks are described as over 150 years old, meaning already standing in 1862. No precise coordinate for the individual trees found this pass, only the general West Woods location (the pin given is the West Woods area, not the trunks); mark approximate honestly. No girth found. A caution for the writer: the blog gives an oak height of approximately 175 feet, which is physically implausible for any oak species (the tallest known oaks in the world top out well under 150 feet) and looks like an error or a mixed-up figure from elsewhere in that source; do not repeat it. Alive: both healthy oaks confirmed by the more recent (professional) source; the blog is 2009 and dated, so if this entry is published a fresher check on current condition would be worthwhile before or shortly after launch.
